modal.title: React Snappy Modal
modal.content: This is an example of the React Snappy Modal in action. It provides a promise-based API that makes handling modal results easy and intuitive.

features.title: Features
features.subtitle: React Snappy Modal is designed to make modal management simple and intuitive with a powerful promise-based API.

promiseBased.title: Promise-based API
promiseBased.description: Use async/await with your modals to handle user interactions in a clean, sequential way without callback hell.

lightweight.title: Lightweight
lightweight.description: Zero dependencies and tiny bundle size to keep your application fast and performant.

customizable.title: Customizable
customizable.description: Easily customize the appearance and behavior of your modals with simple configuration options.

typeSafe.title: Type Safe
typeSafe.description: Built with TypeScript to provide excellent type checking and IntelliSense support.

controlledFlow.title: Controlled Flow
controlledFlow.description: Control the flow of your application by waiting for user input before proceeding with the next steps.

react18.title: React 18+ Compatible
react18.description: Built to work perfectly with the latest versions of React, including concurrent rendering.

alertModal.title: Alert Modal
alertModal.description: Simple alert modals can be used to display information to the user. The modal returns a promise that resolves when the user closes it.

confirmModal.title: Confirmation Modal
confirmModal.description: Confirmation modals let users make decisions. The modal returns the value passed to SnappyModal.close(), making it easy to handle user choices.

formModal.title: Form Modal

gettingStarted.title: Getting Started
gettingStarted.lead: This guide takes you from an empty React app to a modal that returns the user's choice to the code that opened it. It takes about five minutes.

requirements.title: Requirements
body: React Snappy Modal has no runtime dependencies besides React. The package declares React 16.12, 17, and 18 as peer dependencies, and this documentation site runs it on React 19.

Modals are opened with `SnappyModal.show()` and closed by settling a Promise, so you should be comfortable with `async` and `await`. TypeScript declarations ship with the package; there is no separate `@types` package.

install.title: 1. Install the package
body: Install it with your package manager. The stylesheet is bundled and imported automatically when you import `react-snappy-modal`, so there is no CSS file to add.

provider.title: 2. Add SnappyModalProvider
body: `SnappyModalProvider` is where open modals are rendered. Mount it once near the root of your app. Modals are rendered after the provider's children, so they appear on top of your page.
After that, `SnappyModal.show()` can be called from anywhere: components, event handlers, or plain utility functions outside React.

component.title: 3. Write a modal component
body: A modal is an ordinary React component. Inside it, call `useCurrentModal()` to get `resolveModal`. Calling `resolveModal(value)` closes this exact modal and hands `value` to the code that opened it.
The library positions your content and draws the backdrop, but it adds no background, padding, or border to the content. Style the card yourself, as below.

open.title: 4. Open it and await the result
body: `SnappyModal.show(element, options?)` renders the element and returns a Promise. Your function pauses at `await` until the modal closes and then continues with the result. There is no `isOpen` state and no callback prop to wire up.

results.title: What the Promise returns
body: The result depends on how the modal was closed:

rows: Click on the backdrop (when `allowOutsideClick` is true, the default)

flow.title: How it works
body: Under the hood, a single call goes through four steps:
items: `show()` adds the modal to an internal stack, gives it a unique `modalId`, and returns a pending Promise.
`SnappyModalProvider` re-renders and draws every modal in the stack, ordered by `layer`.
Your component calls `resolveModal()`. The modal is removed from the stack and its Promise settles.
The code after `await` runs with the result.

troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
body: Most setup problems fall into one of these cases:

rows: Nothing appears and the code after `await` never runs
`SnappyModalProvider` is not mounted. Make sure it wraps the tree that is on screen. The Promise stays pending until the modal is closed.
Error: useCurrentModal must be used within CurrentModalProvider
`useCurrentModal()` only works in components rendered by `SnappyModal.show()`. Move the hook into the modal component, or close from outside with `SnappyModal.close(value)`.
The content wrapper only handles positioning. Give your root element a background and padding, or pass `className` or `style` in the options.
The modal shows up under a sticky header
Modals use `z-index: 1000` by default. Pass a larger `zIndex` option or lower the other element's z-index.
The page behind the modal cannot scroll
`allowScroll` is false by default: the page is locked while the modal is open and the scroll position is restored on close. Pass `allowScroll: true` for non-blocking panels.

api.title: API Reference
api.lead: Everything exported by `react-snappy-modal` 1.2, with the exact behavior of each call.

exports.title: Exports
body: The default export is the `SnappyModal` class with static methods. The provider and the hooks are named exports.

Renders `component` as a new modal and returns a `Promise<any>` that settles when that modal closes. Every call creates a new modal with its own `modalId`; calling it while another modal is open stacks the new one on top instead of replacing it.
`options` is merged over the defaults listed in the options table below.
Closes one modal and resolves its Promise with `value`. `layerOrId` picks the target: a number (or numeric string) means a layer, anything else is treated as a `modalId`. The default is layer `0`.
When several modals share the target layer, `close()` closes the one that was opened first on that layer, not the newest. If nothing matches, the call does nothing and does not throw.

Works like `close()` but rejects the Promise with `error`. Use it only when the caller should treat the outcome as a failure, and always pair it with `try`/`catch`; otherwise the rejection is reported as unhandled.
Returns `true` while at least one modal is open. It reads the state once and does not cause re-renders. Use `useSnappyModalState()` when a component has to react to changes.
Only available inside a component rendered by `show()`. Returns `resolveModal(value)`, `rejectModal(error)`, the modal's `layer`, and its `modalId`.

`resolveModal` and `rejectModal` target the modal they were rendered in by ID, so they stay correct even when several modals share a layer. Prefer them over the static methods inside modal components.

Subscribes to the modal stack and re-renders when a modal opens or closes. `isShow` is true while any modal is open, and `modalProgress` lists the open modals in render order, each with its `modalId` and resolved `options`.
Renders every open modal after its children and applies the scroll lock. Mount it exactly once near the root of your app.

options.title: Options
body: Pass options as the second argument of `show()`. Each modal keeps its own options.

descriptions.allowOutsideClick: When true, clicking outside the content closes the modal and resolves its Promise with `undefined`. Set it to false when the user must make an explicit choice.
descriptions.allowScroll: When false, the page behind is locked while the modal is open and the scroll position is restored on close. The lock stays on while any open modal has `allowScroll: false`.
descriptions.backdrop: `true` dims the page behind the modal; `false` removes the dimming. The full-screen click area stays either way, so outside clicks still follow `allowOutsideClick`.
descriptions.position: Where the content sits on a 3×3 grid: `top-left`, `top-center`, `top-right`, `center-left`, `center`, `center-right`, `bottom-left`, `bottom-center`, `bottom-right`.
descriptions.zIndex: CSS z-index of the modal area. When omitted, the stylesheet default of 1000 applies.
descriptions.layer: Stacking group. Open modals are sorted by layer, higher layers render on top, and `close(value, layer)` targets a layer.
descriptions.className: Extra class name added to the content wrapper (`.snappy-modal-content`).
descriptions.style: Inline style applied to the content wrapper.

backdropNote.title: Custom backdrop color
body: In version 1.2.1, passing a string as `backdrop` sets the `--snappy-modal-backdrop` CSS variable, but the bundled stylesheet reads `--snappy-modal-backdrop-color`, so the color is not applied. Set the color in your own CSS instead:

targeting.title: How layerOrId is resolved
body: `close()` and `throw()` share the same lookup rules:
items: Numbers and numeric strings such as `1` or `"1"` are layers; any other string is a `modalId`.
For a layer, the modal opened first on that layer is chosen.
If no modal matches, nothing happens.

typescript.title: Typing the result
body: `show()` returns `Promise<any>`. Wrap it in a small generic helper so callers get a precise result type. `undefined` stays in the union because a backdrop click resolves without a value.

asyncConfirmation.summary: Ask for confirmation, then call the API in the same async function, with errors, loading, and double clicks handled.

meta.title: Async Confirm Dialog in React with await - React Snappy Modal Guide
meta.description: Build a promise-based confirm dialog in React: await the user's choice, call an API, report errors, keep the dialog open while saving, and prevent double submits.

asyncConfirmation.title: Guide: Async Confirmation Dialogs
asyncConfirmation.lead: Destructive actions such as deleting a project need an explicit confirmation before the request is sent. This guide builds that flow step by step with `await`, so the whole decision reads top to bottom in one function.

why.title: Why a Promise instead of state
body: With a state-driven modal, the click handler sets `isOpen`, the dialog renders somewhere else, and the real work moves into an `onConfirm` callback. One action ends up spread across three places.
With `SnappyModal.show()`, the handler opens the dialog, waits for the answer, and continues. Local variables stay in scope, early returns work, and a single `try`/`catch` covers the whole flow.

confirm.title: 1. A reusable confirm dialog
body: The dialog only reports the decision. It resolves `true` for confirm and `false` for cancel, and knows nothing about what is being deleted, so the same component works for every confirmation in your app.

outcomes.title: 2. Handle every outcome
body: There are three possible results, and one falsy check covers both ways of cancelling:

errors.title: 3. Report failures
body: `fetch` does not reject on HTTP errors, so check `response.ok` yourself. When the request fails, show the error with another modal. The user stays in context and the function still ends in one place.

pending.title: 4. Keep the dialog open while saving
body: Sometimes the dialog should stay on screen until the server answers, for example to show progress or a server-side error. Move the request into the modal and resolve only after it succeeds.
Disable the buttons while the request is running, and pass `allowOutsideClick: false` so an outside click cannot close the dialog halfway through.

rejection.title: 5. When to reject instead of resolve
body: Treat cancelling as a normal result and resolve it. Reserve `rejectModal(error)` and `SnappyModal.throw(error)` for real failures the caller has to handle, and always wrap those calls in `try`/`catch`; an uncaught rejection surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection.

doubleOpen.title: 6. Prevent opening the same dialog twice
body: A fast double click runs the handler twice and stacks two identical dialogs. Return early when `SnappyModal.isShow()` is true, or keep a local in-progress flag if other modals may legitimately be open.

checklist.title: Checklist
body: Before shipping a confirmation flow, check that:
items: The dialog resolves a value for every button and never leaves the Promise pending.
Both `false` and `undefined` are treated as cancel.
HTTP errors are detected with `response.ok`, not only network errors.
Destructive dialogs that send requests use `allowOutsideClick: false`.
Any use of `rejectModal` or `SnappyModal.throw` is wrapped in `try`/`catch`.
Repeated clicks cannot open a second dialog.

meta.title: Nested and Stacked Modals in React - React Snappy Modal Layers Guide
meta.description: Open modals on top of modals with react-snappy-modal. Learn how layer, modalId, and zIndex work, why close() can close the wrong modal, and how to target the right one.

modalLayers.title: Guide: Stacking Modals with Layers
modalLayers.lead: Real apps open modals from inside modals: a settings dialog that asks for confirmation, or a form that opens a picker. This guide explains how React Snappy Modal orders stacked modals and how to close the one you mean.

concepts.title: Three different settings
body: Stacked modals involve three settings that are easy to mix up:

rows: A number option, `0` by default. Open modals are sorted by layer, and higher layers render later, on top.
Order groups of modals and target a group with `close(value, layer)`.
A unique ID created for each `show()` call, available from `useCurrentModal()`.
The CSS z-index of the modal area, `1000` by default.
Place modals above other page elements such as sticky headers.

pitfall.title: The common mistake: closing by layer
body: Every modal opens on layer `0` unless you pass another one. If a modal opens a second modal and the second calls `SnappyModal.close()`, the library looks for the first modal on layer 0, which is the parent. The parent closes and the child stays on screen.

currentModal.title: Fix 1: close from inside with useCurrentModal
body: `resolveModal()` targets the modal it was rendered in by ID, so it is correct no matter how many modals share a layer. Make it the default in every modal component. The parent can also await the child and close itself only after the child answers.

explicitLayer.title: Fix 2: give nested modals their own layer
body: When you have to close a modal from outside, for example from a timer or a global keyboard shortcut, open each level on its own layer and pass that layer to `close()`. Naming the layers in one constant keeps the order readable.

byId.title: Fix 3: close a specific modal by ID
body: `useCurrentModal()` also returns `modalId`. Have the modal report it from an effect, wait until it arrives, then pass it to `SnappyModal.close(value, modalId)` to close exactly that modal, even if others share its layer. Don't close before the ID is known: an empty ID is read as layer `0` and closes the first modal there.

outsideClick.title: Outside clicks and scroll lock with several modals
body: An outside click closes the modal whose area was clicked, by ID, and resolves its Promise with `undefined`. Modals underneath stay open.
The page stays locked while any open modal has `allowScroll: false`. It unlocks and restores the scroll position only after the last such modal closes.

state.title: Reacting to the stack
body: `useSnappyModalState()` re-renders whenever the stack changes. Use it to pause global keyboard shortcuts while a modal is open, or to show how many dialogs are stacked.

checklist.title: Checklist
body: When a screen can open more than one modal, check that:
items: `SnappyModal.close()` without arguments is only used when a single modal can be open.
Modals closed from outside have their own `layer` or are closed by `modalId`.
`zIndex` is only used to rise above non-modal page elements, not to order modals.
